notes: Brackets: the booklet does not print the rate schedule. Instructions PDF p.8 Line 24 says 'If Line 23 is less than $60,000, use the tax table ... If line 23 is $60,000 or greater, use the tax schedule at the end of the tax table', but neither the table nor the schedule is in the instructions PDF. The schedule is taken from the statute the table is built on: 30 Del. C. §1102(a)(14), 'For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2013, the amount of tax shall be determined as follows: 2.2% of taxable income in excess of $2,000 but not in excess of $5,000; 3.9% ... in excess of $5,000 but not in excess of $10,000; 4.8% ... in excess of $10,000 but not in excess of $20,000; 5.2% ... in excess of $20,000 but not in excess of $25,000; 5.55% ... in excess of $25,000 but not in excess of $60,000; and 6.6% of taxable income in excess of $60,000.' §1102(d)(1) says the Director's tax tables (for tax table income not over $60,000) 'shall be computed on the basis of the rates prescribed by subsection (a)'. The 0% band from 0 to 2,000 is read from 'in excess of $2,000' in the first band; the statute prints no rate below 2,000.

Brackets, one schedule for every filing status: §1102(a)(14) prints one schedule with no filing-status split, so married_joint repeats single. Instructions PDF p.5 corroborates: 'Generally, separate returns (filing status 3 or 4) will be advantageous if both spouses have Delaware adjusted gross income in excess of $9,400' (joint filers do not get wider bands).

Brackets confirmed against the agency's own figures: FAQ 'Retirement Information' answer, 'Delaware has a graduated tax rate ranging from 2.2% to 5.55% for income under $60,000, and 6.60% for income of $60,000 or over'; FAQ 'Bonds' answer, 'The maximum income tax rate is 6.60% on income of $60,000 or over'. Both match the statute's lowest (2.2%), highest below 60,000 (5.55%) and top (6.6% over 60,000) rates, and the 60,000 split matches Line 24's table/schedule split. The intermediate band starts (5,000, 10,000, 20,000, 25,000) are printed only in the statute.
The fetched statute paragraph (a)(14) has no end date ('For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2013'); no later paragraph in §1102 as fetched changes the rates, so it applies to 2025.

Filing statuses (Form PIT-RES p.1): 1 'Single, Divorced, Widow(er)', 2 Joint, 3 Married & Filing Separate Forms, 4 Married & Filing Combined Separate on this form, 5 Head of Household. A widow(er) files status 1, so qualifying_surviving_spouse takes the status-1 standard deduction.
Taxable income: Line 23 = Line 12 (Delaware AGI) minus Line 22 (total deductions), per column. Line 1 is federal AGI (Form 1040 Line 11).

Standard deduction (Line 20a): 3,250 for statuses 1, 3 and 5; 6,500 for status 2; 3,250 in each of Columns A and B for status 4. Additional standard deduction (Line 21): 2,500 per box checked for 65 or over and for blind, 'a maximum of $5,000 per individual', only with the Delaware standard deduction. If one spouse takes the standard deduction the other must (p.5, p.8). Delaware itemized deductions (Form PIT-RSA) may be taken instead, even if the federal standard deduction was claimed (p.7, p.8).

No personal or dependent exemption deduction is printed. Delaware gives personal credits instead: 110 per exemption (Form PIT-RES p.2 Line 27a 'Enter number of exemptions x $110'; instructions p.8: a joint couple with no dependents enters $220), and 110 more for each of you and your spouse 60 or over on 12/31/2025 (Line 27b). Both are non-refundable (Line 32 'TOTAL NON-REFUNDABLE CREDITS'; Line 33 balance not below 0).

Pension exclusion (Line 6), source of the pension: the booklet says 'Amounts received as pensions from employers (including pensions of a deceased taxpayer) may qualify for an exclusion' (p.6). It draws no line between a Delaware government pension, a federal civil service pension, another state's government pension and a private pension, and sets no Delaware-only limit. So public_pension, public_pension_other_state and private_pension are in the same entries. No source names New York or any other state's pension; this is read from the absence of a limit, not from a sentence naming other states. FAQ: 'the amount of your pension and 401K income that is taxable for federal purposes is also taxable in Delaware. However, persons 60 years of age or older are entitled to a pension exclusion of up to $12,500'.

Pension exclusion, military: under 60, a United States military pension has its own 12,500 cap (box on Form PIT-RES p.1 Line 6, 'Column B if You had a Military Pension'). At 60 or over the worksheet takes 'Amount of pension' with no exception, and the under-60 text calls military retirement 'your pension', so military_pension is in the 60-plus entry's covers.

Pension exclusion, 60 or over: the lesser of 12,500 and (pension + 'eligible retirement income'). Eligible retirement income: 'dividends, capital gains net of capital losses, interest, net rental income from real property and qualified retirement plans (IRC Sec. 4974), such as IRA, 401(k), Keogh plans, and government deferred compensation plans (IRC Sec. 457)' (p.6). A pension is not required: in the booklet's example the secondary taxpayer 'received no pension income' and is 'entitled to a pension exclusion of $4,500' from interest, dividends and gains alone. Income from joint accounts is split equally between spouses (example).

Pension exclusion, under 60, non-military: '$2,000 or the amount of your pension, whichever is less' (p.6). The booklet does not say whether IRA or 401(k) distributions count for a person under 60. It says 'An early distribution from an IRA or pension fund ... does not qualify for the pension exclusion' and 'only one pension exclusion, even if he or she is receiving more than one pension or other retirement distribution', which suggests a non-early IRA distribution might; not settled, so ira_distribution and employer_plan_distribution stay in covers_unclear.

Roth conversions are not mentioned anywhere in the sources: covers_unclear on every pension entry. Annuities are not named either (the Line 1 allocation worksheet's 'Taxable pensions and annuities' is a federal line label only): covers_unclear.

Pension exclusion: one per taxpayer; spouses each get one; one spouse's amount over 12,500 cannot be used by the other (p.6). Age is age on December 31, 2025. Early distributions (1099-R Box 7 code 1, or a federal early-withdrawal penalty on Schedule 2) and employer disability pension reported as wages before minimum retirement age do not qualify (p.6).

Social Security: exempt. Instructions p.7 Line 8a: 'Social Security and Railroad Retirement benefits are not taxable in Delaware and, therefore, should not be included in taxable income. Enter on Line 8a the total of any taxable payments included on Line 1.' Second documents: p.3 Persons 60 or Over Checklist ('Social Security and Railroad retirement benefits are excluded from Delaware taxable income'); FAQ; Form PIT-RES p.1 Line 8a label.

Line 11 (Persons 60 or Over or Disabled), p.7 worksheet: two columns with different tests, recorded as two entries. Line 10 is the form's 'Subtract Line 9 from Line 4' (federal AGI plus Lines 2-3, less Lines 5-8b), which is not a measure in the schema list, so base 'other' with the printed text. Head of household is not named in either worksheet column; not stated.
Higher-education exclusion (Line 8a): distributions from IRAs, 401(k) and 457 plans used the same year for books, tuition or fees of the taxpayer or dependents not yet 26; no dollar cap printed.

Interest on U.S. obligations is subtracted (Line 5, p.5); Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae, Sallie Mae and IBRD interest is not exempt. Interest on other states' obligations is added (Line 2); Delaware municipal bonds are exempt (FAQ 'Bonds').

Printed but not recorded (out of scope: not a standard deduction, exemption, retirement or Social Security relief): 529 contribution exclusion (1,000 individual filers with federal AGI under 100,000; 2,000 joint under 200,000) and ABLE contribution exclusion (5,000 individual, 10,000 joint), Line 8b, p.7; credit for tax paid to other states (Line 28, p.9); volunteer firefighter credit 1,000 (Line 29); child care credit 50% of the federal credit (Line 31); earned income credit (Schedule II).

Lump-sum distributions: §1102(b) imposes a separate tax on the ordinary income portion of a lump-sum distribution, figured on Form PIT-STC (Line 25, p.8); a distribution taxed that way is subtracted on Line 8a. Not recorded as a relief.
Capital gains: no separate rate or deduction is printed; gains are in federal AGI and count as eligible retirement income at 60 or over.
No surtax and no recapture of the lower bands is printed in the booklet or in §1102.
Indexing: neither the booklet nor §1102 says any figure is adjusted for inflation; all not_stated.

reliefs.cap_rule: Worksheet: amount of pension plus amount of 'eligible retirement income' (dividends, capital gains net of capital losses, interest, net rental income from real property, and qualified retirement plans IRC Sec. 4974 such as IRA, 401(k), Keogh and government deferred compensation plans IRC Sec. 457); enter that total or $12,500, whichever is less. One exclusion per taxpayer; spouses each get one; one spouse's excess over $12,500 cannot be used by the other. Income from joint accounts is split equally between spouses. A pension is not required (example: secondary taxpayer with no pension gets $4,500).
